back: A combination of elements from both adaptive and predictive approaches. Useful when there is uncertainty or risk around the requirements.

front: When is a hybrid approach useful?
back: When requirements are uncertain, when deliverables can be split into modules, or when different deliverables are built by different teams.

front: The PMBOK Guide's view on hybrid
back: Most projects today benefit from a hybrid approach: flexibility where conditions change, control where work is predictable.

front: Best fit for defined, repeatable work
back: A predictive approach: plan the work, then work the plan.

front: Best fit for novel, intangible knowledge work
back: An adaptive approach: the solution is discovered through feedback.
Requirements uncertainty (agreement on what is needed) and technical uncertainty (certainty about how to deliver it).
Simple work. Predictive approaches work well.

front: Stacey matrix: complicated or complex zones
back: Adaptive approaches work well: the team discovers the solution iteratively through feedback.
Simple, complicated, complex, chaotic, disorder.
Outcomes emerge through experimentation. Probe, sense, respond. Matches agile.
Expert analysis is needed but outcomes are predictable. A hybrid life cycle may fit.
Agile development followed by a predictive rollout. For uncertain development and a defined, repeatable rollout.
Agile and predictive approaches used at the same time throughout the life cycle. Common during a move toward agile.
A largely predictive approach with an agile component, for the one uncertain part of an otherwise routine project.
A largely agile approach with a predictive component, for an element that is non-negotiable or cannot be done incrementally.
Level 1: predictive dominates. Level 2: both contribute significantly. Level 3: adaptive dominates.
Choose the life cycle or combination that works for the project, its risks and the culture. Revisit the choice periodically.

front: When may agile not be useful?
back: When the organization cannot deliver intermediate value.
Add iterative techniques first, then incremental ones, starting on a less risky project, then move to more complex projects.

front: Three categories of factors for choosing a development approach
back: The deliverable, the project and the organization.
Well-known requirements, costly change, rigorous safety requirements, heavy regulation.
High innovation, unstable scope, value from frequent feedback, delivery in parts, high risk and uncertainty.
A questionnaire scored 1 to 10 and plotted on a radar chart, to discuss whether a project suits a predictive, hybrid or agile approach.
Culture, team and project.

front: Suitability filter: reading the radar chart
back: Center: agile. Middle ring: hybrid. Outside: predictive.

front: Is the suitability filter's result binding?
back: No. It is a conversation tool. The people involved decide, and mismatches are treated as risks.

front: The most common blend of agile approaches
back: Scrum (backlog, roles, events), Kanban (board and WIP limits) and XP (engineering practices).
Hybrid: predictive plus adaptive. Blend: several agile approaches together.

front: Tailoring: work is often interrupted or delayed
back: Make work visible on a kanban board and experiment with WIP limits.
Use test-driven development practices.

front: Tailoring: the team is new to agile
back: Train in the agile mindset and principles first, then in the chosen framework.
Split stories to make them smaller; estimate relatively with the whole team; spike what is not understood.

front: Remedy for poorly refined backlog items
back: Product owner and team workshop stories together; write a definition of ready; split stories.

front: Remedy for an uneven, rush-then-wait flow of work
back: Plan to the team's capacity and no more; stop multitasking; pair, swarm or mob.

front: Remedy for slow improvement in teamwork
back: Capture no more than three improvement items at each retrospective.
